title: How much is my comic worth? How to value a comic book
answer: A comic is worth what a copy in the same grade, with the same label and page quality, recently sold for. To value yours: identify the exact issue and printing, grade it honestly (or use the grade on the slab), then look up recent realised sales at that grade from auction houses and marketplaces. Price guides give a starting point, but sales data at your grade is the real answer. Most comics are worth very little; keys and high-grade copies of collectible books are worth checking carefully.
body:
## Step 1 — identify the book exactly

Title, issue number, publisher and cover date from the indicia, and the printing. A facsimile, later printing or foreign edition is a different book with a different value — see [What is a facsimile edition?](/guides/what-is-a-facsimile-edition).

## Step 2 — grade it honestly

If it is slabbed, the label has done this for you. If it is raw, grade it against the standard in [How are comics graded?](/guides/how-are-comics-graded) and err low: almost everyone over-grades their own books. Note page quality and any restoration; both change the value.

## Step 3 — find realised sales at that grade

The value is what buyers have actually paid, not what sellers are asking. Sources, in rough order of usefulness:

- **Auction house archives** (Heritage, ComicConnect, ComicLink) for graded keys — searchable by issue and grade.
- **Marketplace sold listings** for common and mid-value books.
- **Aggregators** such as GPAnalysis and GoCollect that compile graded sales by grade.
- **Price guides** such as the Overstreet guide for a broad reference, remembering that guide values lag the market.

Compare like with like: same grade, same label colour, similar page quality, and a sale within the last few months. Three or four recent sales tell you more than a single outlier.

## Step 4 — adjust for what the data does not show

- **Page quality**: a cream-paged copy sells below a white-paged one at the same grade.
- **Eye appeal**: centering, gloss and a clean scan bring more within the grade.
- **Label**: restored, qualified and signature copies are priced separately.
- **Census position**: top-of-census copies carry a premium.

## What most comics are worth

The honest answer for the majority of comics printed after 1980 is a few dollars or less, because they were printed in huge numbers and survive in quantity. The value in a typical collection is concentrated in a handful of keys and a few very high-grade copies. See [What makes a comic valuable?](/guides/what-makes-a-comic-valuable).

## Getting a professional opinion

For a collection or a single significant book, an [appraisal](/services/appraisal-and-valuation) gives you a written valuation for sale or insurance, based on realised sales rather than asking prices.

faq.a: It is a well-researched annual reference, but it is published once a year and prices for keys can move a great deal in that time. Use it to identify what is collectible, then check recent sales for the price.

faq.q: Why are asking prices so much higher than sold prices?
faq.a: Because anyone can ask anything. Only sold prices tell you what buyers will pay. Ignore listings that have been sitting unsold.

title: What makes a comic book valuable?
answer: Demand for the issue, scarcity in the grade, and condition. Demand comes from what the issue contains — a first appearance, origin or famous story — and from the character's popularity in films, television and games. Scarcity comes from the era's print run and survival rate. Condition, certified by a grading company, decides where a copy sits within that issue's price range. Age alone does not make a comic valuable.
body:
## 1. Content: what happens in the issue

The single biggest factor. A first appearance of a character who went on to matter is a key issue forever; the issue after it, printed in the same numbers, is worth a fraction. See [What is a key issue?](/guides/what-is-a-key-issue).

## 2. Demand: how many people want it

Demand tracks the character's audience. Films and streaming series bring new buyers to a character's keys; a casting announcement can move a minor key overnight. Demand is also why Marvel and DC keys dominate the top of the market: their characters have the largest audiences.

## 3. Scarcity: how many copies survive

- **Golden Age (1938–1956)**: huge print runs, tiny survival. Many keys have only a few hundred graded copies.
- **Silver Age (1956–1970)**: large runs, better survival; high grades scarce.
- **Bronze Age (1970–1985)**: large runs, good survival; 9.8s scarce relative to demand.
- **Modern Age (1991–)**: mostly plentiful, with exceptions for low-print books and variants.

Check the [CGC census](/guides/what-is-the-cgc-census) to see how many copies exist at each grade.

## 4. Condition and certification

Within an issue, price rises steeply with grade, and the top grades carry a disproportionate premium — see [Why is a 9.8 worth so much more than a 9.6?](/guides/why-is-a-9-8-worth-so-much-more). Third-party grading makes the condition verifiable, which widens the pool of buyers.

## 5. Everything else

- **Page quality**, **pedigree**, **witnessed signatures** by the key creators, and **provenance** add value.
- **Restoration** and **qualified defects** subtract it.
- **Cover art** by a celebrated artist and famous covers add demand independent of the story.

## What does not make a comic valuable

- Age by itself. Most 1970s and 1980s comics are worth a dollar or two.
- "Collector's item" printed on the cover. The 1990s taught the hobby that a book printed in millions of copies is never scarce.
- Sealed polybags, chromium covers, and #1 issues of short-lived titles.

For a valuation of a specific book, see [How much is my comic worth?](/guides/how-much-is-my-comic-worth).

title: Why is a 9.8 worth so much more than a 9.6?
answer: Because 9.8 is the practical top of the scale for almost every comic and the grade most collectors of high-grade books insist on. Supply at 9.8 is a small fraction of supply at 9.6 and below, while demand from set-builders and investors concentrates there, so the price step between 9.6 and 9.8 is usually the largest on the whole scale — often two to five times, and far more for scarce Bronze and Silver Age keys.
body:
## The supply side

Every step up the scale removes copies, but the last step removes the most. A 9.8 must have essentially no defects visible without magnification; a single tiny spine tick or corner blunt drops a book to 9.6. For Bronze Age keys, the census typically shows several times more 9.6 copies than 9.8s. For Silver Age keys, a 9.8 may be one of a handful or simply not exist.

## The demand side

The high-grade market has settled on 9.8 as the standard for modern and Bronze Age books. Collectors building "9.8 sets" will not buy a 9.6, and investors prefer the grade with the deepest, most liquid market. The result is that demand at 9.8 is not just higher than at 9.6 but qualitatively different.

## What this looks like in practice

| Era | Typical 9.6 → 9.8 step |
|---|---|
| Modern Age | Modest, because 9.8 is common |
| Copper and Bronze Age keys | Large: several multiples |
| Silver Age keys | Very large when a 9.8 exists at all |
| Golden Age | 9.8 effectively does not exist for most issues; the steep steps happen lower down |

## What it means for buyers

- If you want a book to enjoy, a 9.4 or 9.6 is visually indistinguishable from a 9.8 and far cheaper.
- If you are buying for resale, the 9.8 premium is where most of the return has historically been — and also where the most risk sits if demand softens.
- Beware of a 9.8 with cream pages or poor centering: the number is the same but the market will notice.

## Pressing and the 9.8 line

Because the difference between 9.6 and 9.8 is often a single pressable bend, [pressing](/guides/is-pressing-restoration) before submission is routine for candidates. That is also why the 9.8 population keeps growing for Bronze and Modern keys.

title: How to sell graded comics: your options compared
answer: You can sell a graded comic directly to a dealer for immediate payment at a wholesale price, consign it to a dealer or auction house that sells it for a commission, or list it yourself on a marketplace and handle photography, shipping and buyer questions. Dealers pay least but fastest; auctions reach the most buyers for significant keys; self-listing keeps the most margin but the most work and risk. Whichever route, verify the certification number and check recent sales at your grade before you set a price.
body:
## Option 1 — sell outright to a dealer

Fastest and simplest. A dealer makes an offer, you accept, you are paid. The offer is below retail because the dealer needs a margin and takes on the risk of selling. Best for common books, when you need money now, or when the difference is small enough not to matter. Ask for the offer to be itemised.

## Option 2 — consign

The book is listed and sold by a dealer or auction house on your behalf; you receive the sale price minus a commission. You get closer to retail than an outright sale, in exchange for waiting. For significant keys, a major auction house's catalogue reaches buyers you cannot reach yourself. See [What is consignment?](/guides/what-is-comic-consignment) and our [consignment service](/services/consignment-and-brokerage).

## Option 3 — sell it yourself

Marketplaces give you the widest audience and the most control. You handle scans, descriptions, pricing, fees, shipping, insurance and buyer questions, and you carry the risk of returns and payment disputes. Best for sellers with time and a track record.

## Before you sell, whichever route

1. **Verify the slab** against the grader's records: [How to verify a CGC certification number](/guides/how-to-verify-a-cgc-certification-number).
2. **Check recent sales at your grade**: [How much is my comic worth?](/guides/how-much-is-my-comic-worth).
3. **Check the census position** — "none higher" or a low population is your best selling point.
4. **Photograph the slab front and back** in good light with the label readable.
5. **Decide your floor** before anyone makes you an offer.

## Shipping a slab you have sold

Insured, in a box with padding on all sides, with the slab bagged and immobilised. See [How to ship a graded comic](/guides/how-to-ship-a-graded-comic). Damage in transit is the most common dispute in slab sales and is entirely preventable.

## Selling on this marketplace

Approved sellers list graded and raw books here with their own storefronts, linked from every listing; buyers pay through the site and sellers are paid on delivery. [Contact us](/contact) to apply.

title: What is comic consignment, and how does it work?
answer: Consignment means handing your comics to a dealer or auction house that sells them on your behalf and pays you the sale price minus an agreed commission. You keep ownership until the book sells. It usually returns more than an outright sale to a dealer, because the dealer is not buying the risk, but you wait for the sale and depend on the consignee's reach and honesty. Get the commission, the reserve, the timeline and the insurance in writing before you hand over a book.
body:
## How it works

1. You agree terms: commission rate, any minimum price (reserve), how long the consignee will hold the book, who insures it and who pays shipping.
2. You deliver the book. The consignee lists it, markets it, and handles the buyer.
3. When it sells, you are paid the price less the commission, usually within a stated number of days.
4. If it does not sell within the agreed period, it is returned to you or re-listed at a new price.

## What to look for in a consignment agreement

- **Commission** stated as a percentage, with any minimum fee.
- **Reserve or floor price** — the consignee cannot sell below it without your consent.
- **Insurance** while in the consignee's custody and in transit.
- **Payment timing** after the sale.
- **Term** and what happens at the end of it.
- **Grading and pressing decisions** — whether the consignee may press or grade the book, and who pays.

## Consignment vs auction

Auction houses are consignees too, with the sale price set by bidding on a fixed date. An auction gives a definite outcome and the widest exposure for significant keys; a dealer consignment gives you a fixed asking price and more time. Auction commissions are often split between a seller's fee and a buyer's premium.

## When to consign

Consign when the book is valuable enough that the extra return over a dealer's offer is worth waiting for, and when you do not have the audience or the time to sell it yourself. Our [consignment and brokerage service](/services/consignment-and-brokerage) sets out the commission, insurance and payment terms up front.

title: How to use realised sales data to price a graded comic
answer: Pull the last several sales of the same issue at the same grade and label from auction archives and sales aggregators, discard obvious outliers, and price at or slightly above the recent median for a quick sale or at the top of the range if you can wait. Sales more than six to twelve months old may be stale for a key whose demand has changed. Always match label colour and note page quality; a restored or signature copy is not a comparable for a blue label.
body:
## Building a comparable set

A comparable sale (a "comp") matches your book on:

- Issue and printing
- Grade
- Label type (Universal, Signature Series, Restored, Qualified)
- Grading company, ideally — CGC and CBCS prices can differ a little
- Recency

Three to six comps is enough for most books. If you cannot find sales at your exact grade, bracket it: the price sits between the grade below and the grade above, usually closer to the lower one.

## Reading the numbers

- **Median beats mean.** One record sale skews an average.
- **Direction matters.** Sort by date; a book that sold for less each time over a year is falling, however high the peak was.
- **Auction vs fixed price.** Auction results include a buyer's premium in some archives and not others. Check which.
- **Venue.** A sale at a major auction house with a catalogue reaches more bidders than a marketplace listing; prices there can run higher for keys.

## Adjusting

- Whiter pages than the comps: nudge up. Cream or worse: nudge down.
- Top-of-census position: premium.
- Poor centering or a distracting defect visible in the scan: discount, even within the grade.

## Where sales data comes from

Auction houses publish their archives. Sales aggregators compile graded sales across venues by certification grade. Marketplaces show recent sold listings. None is complete on its own; use two.

## Setting the price

For a quick sale, price at the recent median. To maximise, price at the top of the recent range and be willing to wait. For a book that has not sold at your grade in a year, an auction may be the only way to find out what it is worth today.

See also [How much is my comic worth?](/guides/how-much-is-my-comic-worth) and [What is the CGC census?](/guides/what-is-the-cgc-census).

title: Are comic books a good investment?
answer: Some comics — major keys in high grade — have risen in value substantially over the past few decades, and record sales in the millions of dollars have made headlines. But comics are illiquid, uninsured by default, expensive to buy and sell (grading fees, commissions, shipping), and their prices depend on fashion, film release schedules and the wider economy. Treat them as collectibles that can appreciate, not as a substitute for a diversified investment, and never pay a price you would not be happy to own the book at.
body:
## What has actually happened

Graded copies of the biggest keys have set repeated records: Action Comics #1 sold for 3.25 million dollars in April 2021 and, in a different copy, for 6 million dollars in April 2024; Amazing Fantasy #15 in 9.6 brought 3.6 million dollars in September 2021. See [Record comic book sales](/guides/record-comic-book-sales) for the documented list. Below that tier, Bronze Age keys in 9.8 rose sharply through the 2010s and early 2020s, then cooled from the 2021 peak.

## The costs that eat returns

- **Buying**: buyer's premiums at auction, shipping, and grading fees if you buy raw.
- **Holding**: storage, insurance, the risk of damage.
- **Selling**: commissions of a meaningful percentage, or the time cost of selling yourself.

A book has to appreciate materially just to cover the round trip.

## The risks

- **Liquidity.** There is no market maker. Selling a high-value key at a fair price can take months.
- **Concentration.** A single book is a single bet on a single character's popularity.
- **Fashion.** Demand follows films and series; keys spike on announcements and can fall after release.
- **Grade risk** on raw purchases and **resubmission drift** as more 9.8s are created by pressing.
- **Fraud**: fake slabs, undisclosed restoration, counterfeits.

## A sensible approach

1. Buy books you want to own, so a flat market costs you nothing but money you were happy to spend.
2. Prefer major keys in the best grade you can afford; they are the most liquid.
3. Buy graded, verify certification numbers, and keep records.
4. Insure the collection.
5. Keep it a modest share of your assets.

Nothing here is financial advice; it is what experienced collectors do. For a written valuation of what you own, see our [appraisal service](/services/appraisal-and-valuation).

title: The most expensive comic books ever sold: documented record sales
answer: The record for a single comic is 6 million dollars, paid for a CGC 8.5 copy of Action Comics #1 (1938) at Heritage Auctions in April 2024. Other documented milestone sales include a CGC 7.0 Superman #1 at 5.3 million dollars (private sale, 2022), a CGC 9.6 Amazing Fantasy #15 at 3.6 million dollars (Heritage, September 2021), a CGC 8.5 Action Comics #1 at 3.25 million dollars (ComicConnect, April 2021) and a CGC 9.4 Captain America Comics #1 at 3.12 million dollars (Heritage, April 2022).
body:
## Documented record sales

All figures are the reported hammer price including buyer's premium where the auction house reported it that way, in U.S. dollars.

| Date | Book | Grade | Price | Venue |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 2024 | Action Comics #1 (1938) | CGC 8.5 | $6,000,000 | Heritage Auctions |
| 2022 (announced December) | Superman #1 (1939) | CGC 7.0 | $5,300,000 | Private sale via Heritage |
| September 2021 | Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962) | CGC 9.6 | $3,600,000 | Heritage Auctions |
| April 2021 | Action Comics #1 (1938) | CGC 8.5 | $3,250,000 | ComicConnect |
| April 2022 | Captain America Comics #1 (1941) | CGC 9.4 | $3,120,000 | Heritage Auctions |
| August 2014 | Action Comics #1 (1938) | CGC 9.0 | $3,207,852 | eBay (Pristine Comics) |
| March 2022 | Marvel Comics #1 (1939) | CGC 9.4 | $2,427,000 | Heritage Auctions |
| January 2021 | Batman #1 (1940) | CGC 9.4 | $2,220,000 | Heritage Auctions |
| November 2011 | Action Comics #1 (1938) | CGC 9.0 | $2,161,000 | ComicConnect |
| January 2022 | Detective Comics #27 (1939) | CGC 8.0 | $1,500,000 | Heritage Auctions |
| March 2011 | Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962) | CGC 9.4 | $1,100,000 | ComicConnect |

## What the list tells you

- **Golden Age origins dominate.** Superman, Batman and Captain America's first appearances and first solo issues account for most of the top ten. The supply of high-grade copies is tiny and demand is global.
- **Amazing Fantasy #15 is the Silver Age exception.** It is the only post-1950 book in the top tier, because Spider-Man's audience is as large as Superman's and 9.6 copies are almost non-existent.
- **Grade drives the multiple.** The 9.0 Action Comics #1 in 2014 and the 8.5 copies in 2021 and 2024 show the same book at similar grades appreciating with time and venue.
- **Records cluster in 2021–2024.** The pandemic-era collectibles boom produced most of the entries above; the 2024 Action Comics sale showed that the very top of the market held up.

## How to read a record

A record sale is one buyer's decision on one day for one copy — usually a pedigree copy or a top-of-census copy with a story. It sets a ceiling, not a price for every copy of the issue. For pricing an ordinary copy, see [How to use realised sales data](/guides/how-to-read-comic-sales-data).

This list is limited to sales publicly reported by the auction house or platform involved and will be extended as new records are set.

title: How do I insure a comic book collection?
answer: Standard home contents insurance usually caps collectibles at a low amount and pays only depreciated value, so a collection of any size needs either a scheduled rider on your home policy listing the significant books, or a dedicated collectibles policy that covers agreed values, transit and shows. Either way you will need an inventory with grades and certification numbers, photographs, and for the most valuable books a written appraisal.
body:
## Why ordinary contents cover is not enough

Most home policies limit "collectibles" or "paper items" to a small sub-limit, exclude items away from home, and settle at what the insurer decides the item is worth. A single graded key can exceed the sub-limit on its own.

## Your two options

**A scheduled rider** on your existing home policy lists specific items at agreed values. Simple for a handful of significant books; each one needs documentation and the values need updating as the market moves.

**A specialist collectibles policy** insures the whole collection at agreed or blanket values, typically covers books in transit and at conventions, and is priced on the total value. Better for larger collections and for anyone who buys and sells regularly.

## What the insurer will ask for

1. **An inventory**: title, issue, grade, certification number, purchase price and date, current value.
2. **Photographs** of slabs with labels legible.
3. **Appraisals** for high-value books, from a dealer or appraiser who can cite realised sales — see our [appraisal service](/services/appraisal-and-valuation).
4. **Storage details**: where and how the books are kept.

## Keeping it current

Re-value the significant books yearly. Update the inventory when you buy or sell. Keep a copy of the inventory and photographs somewhere other than with the collection.

## Transit and vault storage

When you ship a book, insure the shipment for its full value — carrier insurance has limits and exclusions for collectibles, so check them. For books you do not need at home, [vault storage](/services/vault-storage) keeps them in controlled conditions under our insurance.
